title: Moments of Genuine Connection https://davestuartjr.com/moments-of-genuine-connection-a-piece-of-paper-a-clipboard-and-a-goal/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. proposes a deliberately low-tech habit for building relationships with students: keep a clipboard with a single sheet listing every student's name and track the brief moments in which each child feels known, valued, or respected. He argues the tracking does four things: it ensures every kid is reached, it turns connection into a skill that gets practiced, it strengthens students' sense of belonging, and it raises their view of the teacher's care. The post ties this to his framework of the five key beliefs, especially Belonging and the Care component of Credibility. He then adds a guardrail that connection is a means to mastery of the subject and long-term flourishing, not the point of the class. He finishes by insisting the moments be genuine and consistent, noting that real connection also produces more joy for the teacher.
points: A clipboard roster of all students makes visible which kids have recently been connected with and which have been missed, so no one slips through.
Genuine connection is framed as a complex skill, more like painting than tying a shoe, that improves only through tracked, deliberate practice.
Short connection moments cultivate the Belonging belief and raise students' perception of teacher Care, one component of Credibility.
Connection is subordinate to teaching the discipline; the point is mastery in service of long-term flourishing.
Because the moments must be genuine, the practice also increases the odds of joy for the teacher.
quotes: We connect with every kid. Using a clipboard and a single sheet of paper with all 120 or so of my students’ names, I can quickly see who I’ve connected with lately, and who I haven’t.

Genuinely connecting with a child — and by this, I mean creating a 1-3 minute situation in which that child feels known, valued, or respected — is a skill. Complex, yes — it’s more like painting a picture than tying your shoes — but a skill nonetheless.
I want all of my students to believe that people like them do work like the work we’ll do in my class. Not only do we do the work — we do it with care.

Moments of genuine connection aren’t resource-intensive; they don’t require intensive planning or huge swaths of our time. Financially, they’re free — zero drain on the budget. Except for the clipboard.

Before you dive in, a quick reminder: The point of your class isn’t moments of genuine connection. If we spend all our time and energy connecting with kids and none of it teaching them to master our course material, then we’re forsaking the call.

I don’t send my children to school each day hoping that they’ll connect with the teacher. I assume that the teacher will work to connect with my child so as to maximize my child’s growth in that teacher’s class, which will in turn increase her odds of flourishing long-term.

And don’t forget to make them real — the word genuine is there for a reason. Because when they’re genuine, one more cool thing starts to happen besides the bulleted list above: we increase the odds that, today, there will be moments of joy for us.
